blocks.prompt: The Camel That Carries Its Lunch on Its Back
blocks.text: Everyone thinks a camel's hump is a water tank. It is not. A hump is a big lump of fat, and fat is food the camel saves for later. When a camel has not eaten for a long time, its humps get floppy and small. Some camels have one hump. Some have two. This one has two. A camel keeps water in its blood, not in its humps. It can drink a whole bathtub of water in about ten minutes. Then it can walk for days without another drink. Its feet are wide and flat, so it does not sink in the sand.

blocks.prompt: What the Hump Is Really For
blocks.text: Ask most people what is inside a camel's hump and they will say water. They are wrong. A hump is a mound of fat, and fat is stored food. When a camel goes a long time without eating, its body burns the fat and the hump droops over to one side like a half empty bag. Count the humps and you can name the camel. A dromedary has one hump and lives in the hot deserts of Africa. A Bactrian camel has two and lives in Central Asia, where winter can drop far below freezing. So where does the water go? Into the camel itself. A thirsty camel can drink about thirty gallons in ten minutes, more than a bathtub holds. The water spreads through its blood and its body, never into the humps. Keeping fat in one tall pile is clever for another reason. If that fat were spread under the skin like a blanket, the camel would cook in the sun. Piled up in a hump, it leaves the rest of the body free to let heat escape. A camel has other desert tools. It can shut its nostrils against blowing sand. It has two rows of eyelashes and a clear third eyelid that wipes each eye like a windshield wiper.

notes: Camelus bactrianus: two humps

blocks.prompt: Built for the Worst Place on Earth
blocks.text: A camel is not a horse that got used to the heat. It is a machine built, piece by piece, for a place that kills. Start with the hump. A dromedary carries one, a Bactrian carries two, and in both cases it is fat, not water. Fat is a food reserve. Stack it in a mound on the back and the rest of the camel stays uninsulated, free to dump heat into the air. Spread that same fat evenly under the skin and the animal would roast. Now the temperature. You and I hold one steady number, and if we drift more than a degree or two we are sick. A camel lets its body temperature slide. Overnight it cools to about 93 degrees Fahrenheit. Through the morning the sun heats it up to 106 before the camel bothers to sweat at all. Every hour it does not sweat is water it does not spend. The blood is strange too. Most animals carry round red blood cells. A camel's are oval, and they can swell to more than twice their size without bursting. That matters at the well. A thirsty camel can drink about thirty gallons in ten minutes, a flood of water that would burst an ordinary animal's cells. The camel's cells simply stretch. And it can afford to run dry. Most mammals are in serious trouble after losing about fifteen percent of their body water. A camel can lose a quarter of its water and keep walking, then drink it all back in one visit. None of this is magic. It is a long list of small solutions to one problem: there is almost no water here, and the sun is not going to stop.

blocks.prompt: The Ship of the Desert Came From the Snow
blocks.text: Everything you know about the camel points to sand. The name means desert. The picture means dunes. The truth is stranger, and it begins in the snow. Camels did not evolve in Arabia or the Gobi. They evolved in North America, more than forty million years ago, and for most of their history that is the only place they lived. Some of them eventually walked west across the Bering land bridge into Asia, and their descendants became the camels we know. Others walked south and became llamas, alpacas, and vicunas. The ones that stayed home died out about eleven thousand years ago. There are no wild camels in America, and yet America is where camels are from. Then, in 2006, researchers digging on Ellesmere Island, high in the Canadian Arctic, pulled fragments of a leg bone out of the frozen ground. Protein analysis identified it as a camel. It was about three and a half million years old, and at the time it lived, Ellesmere was not desert. It was a cold boreal forest with long dark winters and snow. That find changed the reading of the camel's body. Consider what a camel carries. A hump of fat is a food store for a season when nothing grows, and an Arctic winter is exactly that. Wide, splayed, padded feet spread the animal's weight so it does not sink, and snow needs that as much as sand does. Enormous eyes gather light, useful in a winter that barely gets any. A coat that insulates against heat also insulates against cold. If that reading is right, the camel is not a desert invention at all. It is a survivor of hard winters that later found the same toolkit worked in a hard summer. Fat, feet, eyes, and coat did not change jobs. The scenery changed around them. The camel's later story belongs to people. The two humped Bactrian was domesticated in Central Asia and the one humped dromedary in Arabia, both around four to five thousand years ago, and once loaded, they made trade possible across the Sahara and along the Silk Road, carrying salt, cloth, and ideas between worlds that could not otherwise reach each other. In the 1800s, settlers shipped camels to Australia to open the outback, then abandoned them when trucks arrived. Hundreds of thousands of their descendants are still out there, thriving in a country their ancestors never saw.

meta.templateLabel: The Camel That Carries Its Lunch on Its Back

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Camelus bactrianus: two humps, Central Asia
Camelids first appear in North America about 40 million years ago
A Paracamelus fossil was found on Ellesmere Island at 78 degrees north
Identified by collagen surviving inside the bone
Oval red blood cells swell past twice their volume
Wild Bactrian camels: fewer than about 1,000 left

blocks.prompt: Two Famous Facts About the Camel, Both Wrong
blocks.text: Two claims about the camel are famous, and both are wrong. The first is that the hump holds water. The second is that the camel is a creature of the desert. The first error is simple. The second is interesting, because correcting it changes what the animal is. Take the hump first. It is fat. A well fed dromedary carries perhaps eighty pounds of it in a single mound on the spine, and when food runs out the body draws it down until the hump slumps sideways like an emptied sack. Fat is a calorie store, and it is worth asking why the camel keeps its store in one conspicuous pile instead of spreading it under the skin the way a seal or a bear does. The answer is heat. Insulation is the enemy in a hot place. By stacking its reserves in a tower on its back, a camel leaves the rest of its surface bare to the air, free to shed heat, and gains a sunshade over its spine in the bargain. The hump is a fuel tank that also happens to be a parasol. The water is stored in the animal itself. A camel can lose about a quarter of its body water and keep working, a level of dehydration that would kill most mammals twice over. It rations what it has with a stack of unglamorous tricks: it lets its body temperature drift from roughly 93 degrees Fahrenheit at dawn to 106 by afternoon rather than spend water on sweat; its nasal passages are dry enough to pull moisture back out of its own exhaled breath; its kidneys produce a syrupy urine and its gut returns droppings so dry they will burn. Then, at the well, it reverses all of it. A thirsty camel drinks roughly thirty gallons in ten minutes. Such a flood should rupture red blood cells outright, and in most animals it would. Camel red cells are oval rather than round and can swell past twice their volume without failing. Now the second error, which is where the animal gets strange. Camels are not from the deserts of the Old World. They are from North America, where they appeared more than forty million years ago and stayed for most of their history. One branch crossed into Asia by the Bering land bridge and became the dromedary and the Bactrian; another went south and became the llama and its cousins; the branch that remained in America went extinct at the end of the last ice age. The camel is an American animal with no Americans left. The stranger evidence came out of the ground on Ellesmere Island, at 78 degrees north. Between 2006 and 2010 researchers recovered fragments of a fossil leg bone there and identified it, by the collagen preserved inside, as a camel roughly three and a half million years old. Ellesmere then was no desert. It was a boreal forest that spent months of every year in darkness and snow. Line the camel's equipment up against that world and every piece still fits. A hump of fat carries an animal through a season when nothing grows, which describes a northern winter precisely. Broad padded feet keep a heavy body on top of a soft surface, and snow is as soft as sand. Huge eyes are worth having in a winter with almost no daylight. A coat that holds heat out will hold heat in. So the desert may have been a coincidence. The camel did not invent its toolkit for sand. It inherited a toolkit built for cold and found, tens of millions of years later, that the same fat, feet, eyes, and coat worked just as well in a place that had the opposite problem. The camel did not adapt to the desert so much as the desert happened to fit.
